facts.title: Predicted Before It Was Found
facts.text: In 1869 Dmitri Mendeleev left a gap in his periodic table for a missing element he called "eka-boron," predicting its atomic mass and that it would form an oxide of the type X2O3. When scandium was isolated a decade later, its properties matched Mendeleev's forecast almost exactly, becoming one of the triumphs that convinced chemists the periodic table really worked.

facts.title: Named for Scandinavia
facts.text: Swedish chemist Lars Fredrik Nilson discovered scandium in 1879 while analyzing the rare minerals euxenite and gadolinite at Uppsala University. He named it after Scandinavia (Latin "Scandia"), and the element's symbol Sc and atomic number 21 still anchor it at the top of the transition-metal block.

facts.title: A Surprisingly Lightweight Metal
facts.text: Although it sits among the transition metals, scandium is remarkably light, with a density of about 2.99 grams per cubic centimeter — closer to aluminum than to iron. Combined with a high melting point near 1541 degrees Celsius, this low density is exactly what makes it so prized for high-performance aluminum alloys.

facts.title: The Secret in MiG Jets
facts.text: Adding less than half a percent of scandium to aluminum dramatically refines the metal's grain structure, boosting strength and resistance to cracking during welding. Soviet engineers exploited this in the airframes and welded fuel tanks of MiG-21 and MiG-29 fighter jets, and today the same alloys appear in premium bicycle frames, baseball bats, and lacrosse sticks.

facts.title: It Lights Up Stadiums
facts.text: Scandium iodide is added to high-intensity metal-halide lamps because, when vaporized in the arc, it emits a broad spectrum of light very close to natural daylight. These bright, efficient lamps illuminate sports stadiums, film sets, and large arenas, giving cameras the white balance they need.

facts.title: Rare in Rock, Not in the Cosmos
facts.text: Scandium makes up only about 22 parts per million of Earth's crust, and it is so thinly scattered that it rarely forms concentrated ores of its own. Yet it is comparatively abundant in the Sun and many stars, where spectral lines of scandium are routinely detected — a reminder that crustal scarcity and cosmic abundance are very different things.

facts.title: Forged in Dying Stars
facts.text: The scandium in existence was built inside stars, partly through explosive nucleosynthesis in supernovae where extreme temperatures fuse lighter nuclei. Its single stable isotope, scandium-45, carries 21 protons and 24 neutrons, and is the only naturally occurring form, making scandium one of just a handful of mononuclidic elements.

facts.title: Pulled From Uranium Waste
facts.text: Because scandium so rarely concentrates on its own, most of the world's supply is recovered as a byproduct of processing other ores — including the tailings from uranium mining, and residues from titanium, nickel, and rare-earth extraction. The remote Norwegian mine at Ytterby and deposits in places like Bayan Obo, China, have historically been important sources.

facts.title: No Job in Your Body
facts.text: Unlike iron, zinc, or copper, scandium has no known biological role in humans, animals, or plants, and living cells get along perfectly well without it. It also shows low toxicity and is not readily absorbed, so it poses little hazard in everyday amounts — though, as with any fine metal powder, its dust can be flammable.

facts.title: A Radioactive Tracer in Medicine
facts.text: While stable scandium-45 is biologically inert, artificially made radioactive isotopes such as scandium-44 and scandium-47 are being developed for nuclear medicine. Scandium-44 emits positrons useful for PET imaging, while scandium-47 releases particles that can destroy tumor cells, making the pair attractive for "theranostics" that diagnose and treat cancer with chemically identical tracers.
